newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK lawmakers urge change in utilities' regulation.
newsitem.headline: HK lawmakers urge change in utilities' regulation.

text.p: Hong Kong legislators on Monday urged a change in the Scheme of Control, which regulates utilities in the territory, to deal with an oversupply of power.

During a presentation at which China Light & Power Co Ltd told the Legislative Council of its proposals to deal with the issue, the utility came under criticism for its role in building up assets and causing the oversupply.
"The main problem is the Scheme of Control," Democratic legislator Fred Li told Reuters after the panel meeting.
"The two power companies (China Light and Hongkong Electric Holdings Ltd ), their profits are linked with the fixed assets so they have a tendency to maximise their assets."
Under the Scheme of Control, the permitted profits of both utility companies are a percentage of their fixed assets.
China Light is the sole supplier of electricity to the Kowloon peninsula and the New Territories, while Hongkong Electric is the sole supplier to Hong Kong island.
The government will begin a regular interim review of the Scheme of Control in October.
Consultants recommended last year that China Light halt or delay the commissioning of four of the eight units at its Black Point power plant to deal with the oversupply problem.
China Light submitted a report on the costs of a deferral to the government earlier this month.
While China Light told the Legislative Council meeting that the costs of deferring construction at Black Point would be too high, legislators said consumers were paying the price for the oversupply.
"It will be detrimental to the consumers in the long run," said Li.
In its report, China Light proposed alternatives for dealing with overcapacity, which included transferring excess power to Hongkong Electric.
But legislators said under the proposal, China Light would bear no responsibility for its role in overestimating demand.

"So far in the meeting, China Light is trying to sell us the proposal but it is not giving us confidence or a strong reason to buy it," said Democratic legislator Anthony Cheung. "China Light did not say anything about bearing responsibility."

Legislators also questioned provisions in the Scheme of Control that allow China Light to include investments related to units five and six at Black Point in the calculation of its net asset value, thereby boosting its potential permitted profits.
"The Democratic Party will strongly urge the government to include a clause deleting some unnecessary assets into the Scheme of Control," Li said after the meeting.
The government has also asked for more information concerning China Light's proposals before a decision is made.
"We are still waiting for China Light to supply us with more information," said Stephen Ip, Secretary for Economic Services.
More discussion will take place in the Legislative Council on March 10 over the feasibility of China Light transfering electricity to Hongkong Electric.
Hongkong Electric reiterated its position on Sunday that it has no intention of buying excess power supply from China Light.
